newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania security force slips to week of April 14.
newsitem.headline: Albania security force slips to week of April 14.

text.p: Albania's hopes for immediate deployment of an Italian-led security force to protect aid have slipped somewhat after Rome said troop would not reach the strife-torn Balkan country until April 14 at the earliest.
Tirana, racked by weeks of banditry, looting and insurrection, has been urging the fastest possible action since the U.N. Security Council approved the force a week ago.

Italy's foreign ministry said on Friday the multinational force of up to 6,000 troops "should begin deploying in the week starting April 14 in parallel with the arrival of international humanitarian aid".

"The date has slipped slightly. But it still seems on track," one diplomat said. On Monday, Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta had said the force could start deploying in the former Stalinist state by April 10.
Albania says the multinational force, which is to secure two key ports and Tirana airport to help safeguard supplies of food and medicines, is an important step towards normality.
Italy is expected to provide between 2,000 and 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark say they are also considering participation.
Many southern towns are controlled by rebel councils after central government authority collapsed last month amid an armed uprising triggered by anger over the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes.

President Sali Berisha faces new political headaches alongside the unrest after a group of 20 parliamentarians from his right-wing Democratic party issued a challenge, saying they would no longer "accept the diktat of the president".
Accusing Berisha of amassing too much power, their criticism was the strongest towards the former heart surgeon from his own ranks since Albania plunged close to anarchy last month.

The political in-fighting adds to the problems faced by the U.N.-approved force. The breakaway parliamentarians stopped short of a formal split with their party, which won 122 seats out of 140 in parliament in elections last year.

Berisha, in a meeting with a special envoy of Pope John Paul on Friday, reiterated his pledge to hold new elections in June to help resolve the crisis. Southern rebels are demanding his immediate resignation.

"I think that the only road to restore order and stability in the country...is the free and fair elections monitored by the Council of Europe, OSCE and other internatioanl organisations," Berisha said.

Western governments criticised last year's election as unfair following a report by election monitors of the OSCE (Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe), who said the poll failed to meet international standards.
Albanian children are due to meet in the city centre in a rally organised by the U.N. Childrens' Fund (UNICEF) on Saturday to express hope for an end to violence.
"During the past few weeks, children have too often been provided with weapons, never with a voice," a UNICEF statement said.
